content.text:
3.1 Reema's Curiosity
One lazy afternoon, Reema was flipping through an old book when, whoosh!, a piece of paper slipped out and floated to the floor. She picked it up and stared at the strange symbols all over it. "What is this?" she wondered.
She ran to her father, holding the paper as if it were a secret treasure. He looked at it and smiled. "Around 4000 years ago, there flourished a civilisation in a region called Mesopotamia, in the western part of Asia, containing a major part of the present-day Iraq and a few other neighbouring countries. This is one of the ways they wrote their numbers!"
Reema's eyes lit up, "Seriously? These strange symbols were numbers?"
Since when have humans been counting? What was their need for counting? What were they counting?
Since when have people been writing numbers in the modern form?
How would the Mesopotamians have written 20? 50? 100?

content.text:
1. Predict first: if you had never seen our digits, how would you write the number of days in a month?
2. Reema's page shows numbers written about 4000 years ago, with no digits we would recognise.
3. Her questions are ours too: why did people count, what did they count, and how did they write it?
4. Keep the last question open: how would those people have written 20, 50 or 100? We answer it in the last part of the chapter.

media.title: Stick Matching Board
media.context: Class 8 NCERT Ganita Prakash ch 3 A Story of Numbers (Counting Before Numerals). One stick for every cow. Pair them and see what is left. Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.description: Stick Matching Board. One stick for every cow. Pair them and see what is left. Authored rounds, no modes and no question bank: the child acts on the board, then answers; a header with points, hint, sound and home; a task card with Check; a message pill; step dots; Next / Finish; a finish screen with stars. Everything starts raw and changes only when the child acts. English, Hindi and Gujarati.

tool_config.idea: Counting without number names is a one-to-one mapping: every object is paired with exactly one stick, and the sticks left without a partner show what is missing, who has more and how many more are needed. Adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing sticks are joining, pairing off, repeating and sharing out.
tool_config.title: Stick Matching Board
tool_config.screen: A herd of cows in a row, a pile of sticks beside it, and a second herd or pile for comparing. A stick is dragged onto a cow to pair them, and a pair is drawn as a line. Unpaired cows and sticks glow, and no number is printed anywhere until the student has made the pairing.
feedback: A stick dropped on a cow that already has one is returned with the message that each cow gets one stick.
Unpaired sticks and cows glow so the leftover can be seen before any number is said.
A wrong answer shows the pairing again with the leftover sticks counted off one at a time.
tool_config.done_when: All seven cards are done with every pairing one to one and the leftover read correctly.
challenges: In the morning 8 sticks are kept, one for each cow. In the evening 6 cows return and each takes out one stick. How many cows are still missing?
Herd A has 9 cows and herd B has 6 cows. Pair them: which herd has more, and how many more cows does the other need to match it?
Two herds each have 7 cows. Pair them and say what is left over.
Add a pile of 4 sticks and a pile of 5 sticks by joining them. How many sticks are in the joined pile?
Subtract 3 sticks from a pile of 8 by pairing and taking away the pairs. How many sticks are left?
Multiply by repeating a pile of 3 sticks once for each of 4 sticks. How many sticks are there in all?
Divide a pile of 13 sticks into groups of 4. How many full groups are there and how many sticks are left?

hint_ladder.text: Which collection has an object with no partner yet?
Pair one stick with one cow and see what is left over.
Count only the unpaired ones: they answer the question.
The pairing is completed and the leftover is shown, then a new card follows.

student_does: Look at the two collections and predict which has more before pairing anything.
Drag one stick onto each cow, never two sticks onto one cow.
Look at what is left without a partner and say what it means.
Join, pair off, repeat or share out piles of sticks to carry out an operation.

media.description: The five old names eka, dasha, shata, sahasra and ayuta sit in a row, and each fills an empty box with its number. Every step multiplies the number before by ten. Keeko's doubt is that each name is ten more than the one before.

video_script.why: The child sees that the old Indian number names grow by multiplying by ten each time, the same powers of ten we use when we say numbers today.

topics.summary: Counting is a one-to-one mapping between objects and a standard sequence with a fixed order; such a sequence is a number system, and the written symbols in it are numerals. A good system never runs out and is easy to count with.

content.text:
Humans had the need to count even as early as the Stone Age. They were counting to determine the quantity of food they had, the number of animals in their livestock, details regarding trades of goods, the number of offerings given in rituals, etc.
Ancient Indian texts, such as the Yajurveda Samhita, mentioned names of numbers based on powers of 10, almost as we say them orally today. For example, they listed names for the numbers one (eka), ten (dasha), hundred (shata), thousand (sahasra), ten thousand (ayuta), etc., all the way up to 10 to the power 12 and beyond.
The first known instance of numbers being written using ten digits, including the digit 0 (which was then notated as a dot), occurs in the Bakhshali manuscript (c. 3rd century CE).
The Indian number system was transmitted to the Arab world by around 800 CE.
From the Arab world, the Hindu numerals were transmitted to Europe and to parts of Africa by around 1100 CE.
"The ingenious method of expressing every possible number using a set of ten symbols (each symbol having a place value and an absolute value) emerged in India." (Pierre-Simon Laplace)
The most commonly used terminologies for the numbers we use today are 'Hindu numerals', 'Indian numerals', and the transitional 'Hindu-Arabic numerals'.
The shape of the digits 0, 1, 2, ..., 9 used to write numbers in the Indian number system today evolved over a period of time.

content.text:
Worked example: The Yajurveda lists eka, dasha, shata, sahasra and ayuta. Which numbers are these, and how is each one related to the one before it?
1. eka is one and dasha is ten: 10 × 1 = 10.
2. shata is a hundred: 10 × 10 = 100.
3. sahasra is a thousand: 10 × 100 = 1000.
4. ayuta is ten thousand: 10 × 1000 = 10000.
5. Each name is 10 times the one before it, so the names follow powers of 10, just as we say numbers today.
Answer: 1, 10, 100, 1000 and 10000; each is 10 times the one before

content.text:
The Mechanism of Counting
Imagine that we are living in the Stone Age, say, around ten thousand years ago. Suppose we have a herd of cows.
Q1. How do we ensure that all cows have returned safely after grazing? Q2. Do we have fewer cows than our neighbour? Q3. If there are fewer, how many more cows would we need so that we have the same number of cows as our neighbour?
Method 1: We could tackle the questions by using pebbles, sticks or any object that is available in abundance. Let us choose sticks. For every cow in the herd, we could keep a stick.
This way of associating each cow with a stick, such that no two cows are associated or mapped to the same stick is called a one-to-one mapping.
How will you use such sticks to answer the other two questions (Q2 and Q3)?

1. Predict first: with no number names at all, can you tell whether every cow came home?
2. Keep one stick for each cow in the morning. In the evening, take one stick out for each cow that returns.
3. A stick left over means a cow is missing; this pairing, one cow to one stick, is a one-to-one mapping.
4. To compare with a neighbour, pair your sticks with theirs: the unpaired sticks show who has more and how many more are needed.

content.text:
Worked example: In the morning a herder keeps one stick for each cow. In the evening she takes out one stick for each cow that returns, and 2 sticks are left. Her neighbour's stick bundle, paired stick by stick with hers, has 3 sticks without partners. What can she say?
1. Each returning cow removes exactly one stick, so every stick left stands for a cow that did not return.
2. 2 sticks are left, so 2 cows are still missing.
3. Pairing her sticks with the neighbour's sticks one to one, the 3 unpaired sticks are on the neighbour's side.
4. So she has fewer cows than her neighbour, and she needs 3 more cows to have the same number.
Answer: 2 cows are missing; she has fewer cows than her neighbour and needs 3 more

Method 2: Instead of objects, we could use a standard sequence of sounds or names. For example, we could use the sounds of the letters of any language.
An obvious limitation of using only the letters of the English alphabet in this form is that it cannot be used to count collections having more than 26 objects.
How many numbers can you represent in this way using the sounds of the letters of your language?
Method 3: We could use a sequence of written symbols as follows.
I, II, III, IV, V, VI, VII, VIII, IX, X, XI, XII, XIII, XIV, XV, XVI, XVII, XVIII, XIX, XX (Table 1)
Do you see a way of extending this method to represent bigger numbers as well? How?

content.text:
For counting and finding the size of a collection, we need a standard sequence of objects, or names, or written symbols, that has a fixed order. Let us call this standard sequence a number system.
Since there is no end to numbers, the challenge is to come up with an unending standard sequence/number system that is easy to count with.
Using sticks gives an unending standard sequence/number system. However, it is not convenient to count larger collections, as we will need as many sticks as the number of objects being counted.
The standard sequence/number system given in Method 3 was actually the system used in Europe before it got replaced by the Hindu number system. It is called the Roman number system.
The symbols occurring in a written number system are called numerals.

content.text:
1. Predict first: which of the three methods could count a herd of a thousand cows most easily?
2. A number system is a standard sequence with a fixed order; we count by mapping objects to it one to one.
3. Sticks never run out but need one stick per object; letters are easy to say but stop at 26; Roman symbols need new symbols for bigger numbers.
4. The written symbols of a number system are its numerals, like 0, 1, 5, 36 and 193 in ours.

content.text:
Worked example: Compare the three counting methods (sticks, letters a to z, Roman symbols) on two questions: does the sequence ever end, and is it easy to count a large collection with it?
1. Sticks: add one more stick each time, so the sequence never ends; but 500 cows need 500 sticks, which is slow and heavy.
2. Letters: easy to say quickly, but after z there is no next letter, so it ends at 26.
3. Roman symbols: compact, but bigger and bigger numbers keep needing new symbols.
4. None of the three is both unending and easy; that is the challenge a good number system must meet.
Answer: Sticks never end but are slow; letters are quick but end at 26; Roman symbols need ever new symbols

content.publication_text: Suppose you are using the number system that uses sticks to represent numbers, as in Method $1$. Without using either the number names or the numerals of the Hindu number system, give a method for adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing two numbers or two collections of sticks.

content.text:
$1$. To add, put the two collections of sticks together; the joined pile is the sum.
$2$. To subtract, pair each stick of the smaller pile with a stick of the larger pile and take the pairs away; the unpaired sticks are the difference.
$3$. To multiply, lay out the first pile once for every stick of the second pile and join all the copies.
$4$. To divide, keep taking out groups the size of the second pile; the number of groups is the quotient and the sticks that cannot make a full group are the remainder.
Answer: Add by joining, subtract by pairing and removing, multiply by repeating one pile once per stick of the other, divide by taking out equal groups

content.text: One way of extending the number system in Method $2$ is by using strings with more than one letter, for example, we could use '$aa'$ for $27$. How can you extend this system to represent all the numbers? There are many ways of doing it!

content.text:
$1$. After $z$, start again with doubled letters: $aa$, $bb$, $cc$, $\ldots$, $zz$ count the next $26$ objects.
$2$. Then use tripled letters aaa, bbb, $\ldots$, zzz for the next $26$, and so on.
$3$. Another way: after $z$ use $aa$, $ab$, $ac$, $\ldots$, $az$, then $ba$, $bb$, $\ldots$, like the columns of a spreadsheet.
$4$. Either way, longer strings can always be made, so the sequence never runs out.
Answer: One way: a to $z$, then $aa$, $bb$, $\ldots$, $zz$, then aaa, bbb, $\ldots$, zzz and so on; many other ways work

Either way, longer strings can always be made, so the sequence never runs out.

$1$. After $z$, start again with doubled letters: $aa$, $bb$, $cc$, $\ldots$, $zz$ count the next $26$ objects.
$2$. Then use tripled letters aaa, bbb, $\ldots$, zzz for the next $26$, and so on.
$3$. Another way: after $z$ use $aa$, $ab$, $ac$, $\ldots$, $az$, then $ba$, $bb$, $\ldots$, like the columns of a spreadsheet.
$4$. Either way, longer strings can always be made, so the sequence never runs out.
Answer: One way: a to $z$, then $aa$, $bb$, $\ldots$, $zz$, then aaa, bbb, $\ldots$, zzz and so on; many other ways work

topics.summary: Early systems used body parts and tally marks, one mark per object. Counting in groups, in twos for the Gumulgal or in fives for tally marks, made numbers shorter, but one group size alone is still slow for large numbers.

content.text:
3.2 Some Early Number Systems
I. Use of Body Parts: Many groups of people across the world have used their hands and body parts for counting.
II. Tally Marks on Bones and Other Surfaces: One of the oldest methods of number representation is by making notches, marks cut on a surface such as a bone or a wall of a cave. These marks are also called tally marks.
In this method, a mark is made for each object that is being counted.
The Lebombo bone, discovered in South Africa, is an even older tally stick with 29 notches, estimated to be around 44,000 years old.

1. Predict first: is a row of 29 notches easy to read at a glance?
2. Body-part counting points to fingers, wrist, elbow, shoulder and so on, in a fixed order.
3. A tally makes one mark for each object, just like keeping one stick for each cow.
4. Long rows of marks are hard to read, which is why people began to bunch them in groups.

content.text:
Worked example: The Lebombo bone has 29 notches. Group them in fives. How many full groups are there, and how many notches are left over?
1. Count off five notches at a time: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25.
2. That is 5 full groups of five, and 5 × 5 = 25.
3. 29 − 25 = 4, so 4 notches are left over.
4. So the 29 notches read as 5 groups of five and 4 more: 5 × 5 + 4 = 29.
Answer: 5 groups of five and 4 more

content.text:
III. Number Names Obtained by Counting in Twos
A group of indigenous people in Australia called the Gumulgal had the following words for their numbers: 1 urapon, 2 ukasar, 3 ukasar-urapon, 4 ukasar-ukasar, 5 ukasar-ukasar-urapon, 6 ukasar-ukasar-ukasar.
The numbers are counted in 2s, using which the number names are formed: 3 = 2 + 1, 4 = 2 + 2, 5 = 2 + 2 + 1, 6 = 2 + 2 + 2.
Gumulgal called any number greater than 6 ras.
Despite being so far apart geographically, and with no trace of contact between them, these three groups have developed equivalent number systems!

content.text:
1. Predict first: if urapon is 1 and ukasar is 2, what might the name for 3 be?
2. Each name is made of twos and at most one extra one: 3 is ukasar-urapon, 2 + 1.
3. 4 is two ukasars, 5 is two ukasars and an urapon, 6 is three ukasars.
4. Beyond 6 they just said ras, many; the Bakairi and the Bushmen counted in twos in the same way.

content.text:
A general form which this idea has taken in different number systems is as follows: count in groups of a certain number (like 2 in the case of Gumulgal's system), and use the word or symbol associated with this group size to represent bigger numbers.
Some of the commonly used group sizes in different number systems have been 2, 5, 10 and 20.
Up to what group size could you immediately see the number of objects without counting? Most humans find it difficult to count groups having 5 or more objects in a single glance.
What could be the difficulties with using a number system that counts only in groups of a single particular size? How would you represent a number like 1345 in a system that counts only by 5s?

A general form which this idea has taken in different number systems is as follows: count in groups of a certain number (like 2 in the case of Gumulgal's system), and use the word or symbol associated with this group size to represent bigger numbers.
Some of the commonly used group sizes in different number systems have been 2, 5, 10 and 20.
Up to what group size could you immediately see the number of objects without counting? Most humans find it difficult to count groups having 5 or more objects in a single glance.
What could be the difficulties with using a number system that counts only in groups of a single particular size? How would you represent a number like 1345 in a system that counts only by 5s?

content.text:
1. Predict first: how many dots can you see at a glance without counting, 3, 6 or 10?
2. Most people see up to about 4 at once; 5 or more need counting, so marks were bunched in fives.
3. Counting in groups of one size, such as 2 or 5, shortens a long row of marks.
4. But a large number still needs a huge number of groups, so one group size alone is not enough.

content.publication_text: In a system that counts only by $5s$, how would $1345$ be written? How many group symbols are needed?

content.text:
$1$. Find how many fives make $1345$: $1345 \div 5 = 269$.
$2$. Check: $269 \times 5 = 1345$, so nothing is left over.
$3$. So $1345$ needs the symbol for five written $269$ times.
$4$. That is far too many symbols to write or read, so a single group size soon becomes cumbersome.

content.text: A group of indigenous people in a Pacific island use different sequences of number names to count different objects. Why do you think they do this?
content.question: A group of indigenous people in a Pacific island use different sequences of number names to count different objects. Why do you think they do this?
content.question_tex: A group of indigenous people in a Pacific island use different sequences of number names to count different objects. Why do you think they do this?
content.publication_text: A group of indigenous people in a Pacific island use different sequences of number names to count different objects. Why do you think they do this?

content.text:
$1$. Think about what was being counted: fish, coconuts, canoes, days.
$2$. Things that come in bunches or pairs may be easier to count in their own groups.
$3$. A separate sequence also tells the listener what kind of object is meant.
$4$. So the sequences may follow how each kind of object is usually grouped, traded or used.
Answer: Open answer: for example, each kind of object is grouped or traded in its own way, and the name also tells what is being counted

media.context: Class 8 NCERT Ganita Prakash ch 3 A Story of Numbers (Landmarks and Bases). Split the number. Build it from Roman tiles. Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.description: Roman Numeral Builder. Split the number. Build it from Roman tiles. Authored rounds, no modes and no question bank: the child acts on the board, then answers; a header with points, hint, sound and home; a task card with Check; a message pill; step dots; Next / Finish; a finish screen with stars. Everything starts raw and changes only when the child acts. English, Hindi and Gujarati.

tool_config.idea: A Roman numeral groups a number into landmark numbers 1, 5, 10, 50, 100, 500, 1000, largest first, and adds their values. A smaller symbol written before a larger one is subtracted, so IV is 4 and XC is 90.
tool_config.title: Roman Numeral Builder
tool_config.screen: A target number at the top, a tray of landmark tiles I, V, X, L, C, D and M, a build row where tiles are placed left to right, and a running total under the row that updates as each tile is placed.
feedback: A wrong total shows each tile's value under it, so the stray tile is easy to see.
Four of the same tile in a row is flagged and the subtractive pair is suggested.
A subtractive pair that the Romans did not use, such as IC, is rejected with the reason.
tool_config.done_when: All six cards are done with each built numeral matching its target.
challenges: Build 1222 from landmark tiles.
Build 2999 using subtractive pairs.
Build 302 and 715.
Read MMCCCLXVII back as a number.
Add CCXXXII and CCCCXIII by joining tiles and regrouping.
Which is greater, CDXC or CCCC? Build both and compare totals.

hint_ladder.text: Which landmark numbers fit inside the target?
Start with the largest landmark that fits and take it away.
Repeat with what is left, using a pair like XC where four symbols would be needed.
The numeral is built tile by tile with the total shown, then a new card follows.

Drag landmark tiles into the build row, largest first.
Use a subtractive pair such as CM, XC or IV where four of a symbol would be needed.
Check the running total against the target and read the finished numeral back.

media.description: A number is broken into Roman landmark numbers, taking the largest that fits again and again. The video does this for 2367 and then writes one Roman symbol for each landmark. Keeko's doubt is that the digits can be written in Roman side by side.

marks.book: the small title card From your book appears

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about the Roman number system.
People who used Roman numbers calculated with a tool called the abacus.
<bookmark mark='syms'/>Its basic symbols stand for one, five, ten, fifty, one hundred, five hundred and one thousand.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>We want two thousand three hundred sixty seven as a sum of these values.
How do we then write it as a Roman numeral?
beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; the number 2367 appears with the Roman symbols I, V, X, L, C, D, M and their values 1, 5, 10, 50, 100, 500, 1000 under them; a question mark appears Photo: A wooden abacus frame with beads pushed to the sides

marks.think: Kiko sits at the corner of the board and the question mark glows

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.
beats.on_screen: the number and the symbols hold still and the question mark glows

marks.big: see, dee and em are joined to one hundred, five hundred and one thousand
marks.term: the label landmark numbers appears over the row
marks.small: eye, vee, ex and el are joined to one, five, ten and fifty

narration: <bookmark mark='small'/>Eye is one, vee is five, ex is ten, and el is fifty.
<bookmark mark='big'/>See is one hundred, dee is five hundred, and em is one thousand.
<bookmark mark='term'/>Numbers that have a new basic symbol are called landmark numbers.
beats.on_screen: the symbols move to the stage; each symbol is joined to its value; the label landmark numbers appears over the row

marks.given: the facts are written as the given

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the number two thousand three hundred sixty seven, and the seven landmark numbers.
beats.on_screen: Given: the number 2367; the Roman landmark numbers 1, 5, 10, 50, 100, 500, 1000

marks.find: the words To find are written under the given

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to write it as a sum of landmark numbers, and then as a Roman numeral.
beats.on_screen: To find: 2367 as a sum of landmark numbers, and as a Roman numeral

marks.m1: two blocks of 1000 are cut from 2367 and 2367 − 2000 = 367 is written
marks.m2: a block of 500 is tried against 367 and does not fit

narration: <bookmark mark='s1'/>Step one, take as many thousands as possible.
<bookmark mark='m1'/>Two thousands fit in two thousand three hundred sixty seven, because three thousands would be too many.
Taking them away leaves three hundred sixty seven.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>No five hundred fits in that, because it is too big.
beats.on_screen: Step 1: two 1000s fit: 2367 − 2000 = 367; no 500 fits in 367

marks.m3: three blocks of 100 are cut from 367 and 367 − 300 = 67 is written
marks.m4: one block of 50 is cut from 67 and 67 − 50 = 17 is written

narration: <bookmark mark='s2'/>Step two, go on to the hundreds and the fifty.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Three hundreds fit, because four hundreds would be too many.
Three hundred sixty seven take away three hundred leaves sixty seven.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>One fifty fits, so sixty seven take away fifty leaves seventeen.
beats.on_screen: Step 2: three 100s fit: 367 − 300 = 67; one 50 fits: 67 − 50 = 17

marks.m5: one block of 10 is cut from 17 and 17 − 10 = 7 is written
marks.m6: one block of 5 is cut from 7 and 7 − 5 = 2 is written, and two blocks of 1 remain

narration: <bookmark mark='s3'/>Step three, finish with the smaller landmark numbers.
<bookmark mark='m5'/>One ten fits, so seventeen take away ten leaves seven.
<bookmark mark='m6'/>One five fits, so seven take away five leaves two.
Those are two ones.
beats.on_screen: Step 3: one 10 fits: 17 − 10 = 7; one 5 fits: 7 − 5 = 2, which is two 1s

marks.m8: the rest of the sum, + 50 + 10 + 5 + 1 + 1, is written after it
marks.m9: M M appears under the two 1000s, C C C under the three 100s, and L under the 50
marks.m10: X appears under the 10, V under the 5, and I I under the two 1s

narration: <bookmark mark='s4'/>Step four, write the sum, and then write one symbol for each landmark number.
<bookmark mark='m7'/>One thousand plus one thousand plus one hundred plus one hundred plus one hundred.
<bookmark mark='m8'/>Then fifty plus ten plus five plus one plus one.
<bookmark mark='m9'/>Two thousands give em em, three hundreds give see see see, and fifty gives el.
<bookmark mark='m10'/>Ten gives ex, five gives vee, and the two ones give eye eye.
Each landmark number has its own symbol, so the numeral matches the sum.
beats.on_screen: Step 4: 2367 = 1000 + 1000 + 100 + 100 + 100 + 50 + 10 + 5 + 1 + 1; one symbol for each landmark number

marks.res: the sum glows, term by term

narration: <bookmark mark='pay'/>Two thousand three hundred sixty seven is em em see see see el ex vee eye eye.
<bookmark mark='res'/>The sum has two thousands, three hundreds, one fifty, one ten, one five and two ones.

marks.kr1: Kiko appears at bottom right with a blue question box
marks.kr2: the question appears in the box

narration: <bookmark mark='kr1'/>Kiko has one question to ask.
<bookmark mark='kr2'/>What is the real-life use case?
Old clock towers often show Roman symbols on the clock face.
To read vee eye eye, we add five and one and one, which is seven.
beats.on_screen: Kiko at bottom right, blue question box beside him with the question; the clock face of a tower, with vee eye eye shown as five plus one plus one Photo: An old stone clock tower in an Indian town

marks.km1: Kiko appears at bottom right with a blue question box
marks.km2: the question appears in the box

narration: <bookmark mark='km1'/>Kiko has one question to ask.
<bookmark mark='km2'/>What mistake do some students make here?
Some students think we can write two, three, six and seven in Roman symbols, side by side.
But Roman symbols have no places, so all the symbols in a row are added together.
Two, three, six and seven added together make only eighteen, so that row cannot be the numeral.
beats.on_screen: Kiko at bottom right, blue question box beside him with the question; the four small Roman numerals in a row, with their sum eighteen and a red cross

video_script.wrong_move: Kiko writes the Roman symbols for 2, 3, 6 and 7 side by side. Roman symbols have no places, so the row only adds up to 18.
maths_rules: I = 1, V = 5, X = 10, L = 50, C = 100, D = 500, M = 1000; these are the landmark numbers
one 10 fits: 17 − 10 = 7; one 5 fits: 7 − 5 = 2, which is two 1s
one symbol for each landmark: M M C C C L X V I I, which is MMCCCLXVII
video_script.payoff_line: Two thousand three hundred sixty seven is em em see see see el ex vee eye eye

final_answer.spoken: two thousand three hundred sixty seven is one thousand plus one thousand plus one hundred plus one hundred plus one hundred plus fifty plus ten plus five plus one plus one, written as em em see see see el ex vee eye eye

video_script.substitution: Take the largest landmark number that fits, take it away, and repeat on what is left; then replace each landmark with its symbol.
video_script.wrong_answer: write two, three, six and seven in Roman symbols, side by side

media.description: Two Roman numerals are added by counting the symbols of each kind and swapping every full group for a bigger symbol. The video does this for the numerals for 232 and 413, and checks the sum with our own numbers. Keeko's doubt is that the symbols can stay in one long row.

video_script.why: The child sees that Roman numerals can be added by gathering the symbols and regrouping, with no need to change them to our numerals.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about adding Roman numerals.
People who used Roman numbers calculated with a tool called the abacus.
<bookmark mark='nums'/>Here are the Roman numerals for two hundred thirty two and four hundred thirteen.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>How can we add them without changing them to Hindu numerals?

marks.m2: the X pile is counted and 3 + 1 = 4 is written

narration: <bookmark mark='s1'/>Step one, count the symbols of each kind.
<bookmark mark='m1'/>Two see and four see make six see.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Three ex and one ex make four ex.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Two eye and three eye make five eye.
We add the counts of each kind because the symbols have fixed values.
beats.on_screen: Step 1: count the symbols: C's 2 + 4 = 6, X's 3 + 1 = 4, I's 2 + 3 = 5

marks.m4: the five I symbols are circled and swapped for one V

narration: <bookmark mark='s2'/>Step two, start with the small symbols.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Five eye make one vee, so we swap the five eye for one vee.
beats.on_screen: Step 2: five I's make one V

marks.m5: the four X symbols are replaced by an X placed before an L, with a note that 40 is 10 less than 50

narration: <bookmark mark='s3'/>Step three, look at the four ex.
<bookmark mark='m5'/>Four ex are written as ex el, because forty is ten less than fifty.
beats.on_screen: Step 3: four X's are written XL, ten less than fifty

marks.m6: five of the six C symbols are circled and swapped for one D, and one C is left
marks.m7: the D and the left over C are written together as DC

narration: <bookmark mark='s4'/>Step four, look at the six see.
<bookmark mark='m6'/>Five see make one dee, and one see is left.
<bookmark mark='m7'/>Six see are written dee see, because dee comes first.
beats.on_screen: Step 4: six C's: five C's make a D, one C is left, so DC

marks.res: the symbols of the answer add back to 645

narration: <bookmark mark='pay'/>The sum is dee see ex el vee.
<bookmark mark='chk'/>Check with our numbers.
Two hundred thirty two plus four hundred thirteen makes six hundred forty five.
<bookmark mark='res'/>Dee see ex el vee is five hundred, one hundred, forty and five.
That also makes six hundred forty five.

narration: <bookmark mark='km1'/>Kiko has one question to ask.
<bookmark mark='km2'/>What mistake do some students make here?

But a row with five eye, or five see, is not finished.
Each full group of five becomes a bigger symbol, so five eye make one vee.

count the symbols: C's 2 + 4 = 6, X's 3 + 1 = 4, I's 2 + 3 = 5
5 I's make 1 V

6 C's: 5 C's make a D and 1 C is left, so DC
the sum is DC, XL and V together: DCXLV = 500 + 100 + 40 + 5 = 645

narration: <bookmark mark='s1'/>Step one, count the symbols of each kind.
<bookmark mark='m1'/>One el and one el make two el.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Three ex and two ex make five ex.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: 5 I's make a V, so 3 V's; 2 V's make an X and 1 V stays; X's are now 5 + 1 = 6

narration: <bookmark mark='s3'/>Step three, look at the six ex.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: 5 X's make an L and 1 X stays; L's are now 2 + 1 = 3

topics.summary: Roman numerals group a number into landmark numbers, as many of the largest as possible first. Adding works by counting and regrouping symbols, but the group sizes change from landmark to landmark, so multiplying is hard.

content.text:
IV. The Roman Numerals
To get the Roman numeral for any number till 39, it is first grouped into as many 10s as possible, the remaining is grouped into as many 5s as possible, and finally the remaining is grouped into 1s.
Example: Let us take the number 27. 27 = 10 + 10 + 5 + 1 + 1. So, 27 in Roman numerals is XXVII.
Instead of representing 50 as XXXXX, a new symbol is given to it: L. Following the way the number 4 is represented as 1 less than 5, that is, as IV, 40 is represented as 10 less than 50, that is, as XL.
Let us call all these numbers that have a new basic symbol as landmark numbers.
I 1, V 5, X 10, L 50, C 100, D 500, M 1,000.
Consider the number 2367. Writing it as a sum of landmark numbers starting from 1000 such that we take as many 1000s as possible, 500s as possible, and so on, we get 2367 = 1000 + 1000 + 100 + 100 + 100 + 50 + 10 + 5 + 1 + 1.
This system seems to have evolved out of the ancient Greek number system in around the 8th century BCE in Rome, and evolved over time.

content.text:
Worked example: Write 2367 as a sum of Roman landmark numbers and then as a Roman numeral.
1. Two 1000s fit in 2367: 2367 − 2000 = 367. No 500 fits in 367.
2. Three 100s fit: 367 − 300 = 67. One 50 fits: 67 − 50 = 17.
3. One 10 fits: 17 − 10 = 7. One 5 fits: 7 − 5 = 2, which is two 1s.
4. So 2367 = 1000 + 1000 + 100 + 100 + 100 + 50 + 10 + 5 + 1 + 1.
5. Writing one symbol for each landmark, 2367 is written as MMCCCLXVII.
Answer: 2367 = 1000 + 1000 + 100 + 100 + 100 + 50 + 10 + 5 + 1 + 1, written as MMCCCLXVII

concepts.concept_name: Group a number into landmark numbers

content.text:
Despite the relative efficiency of the Roman system, it doesn't lend itself to an easy performance of arithmetic operations, particularly multiplication and division.
Example: Try adding the following numbers without converting them to Hindu numerals: (a) CCXXXII + CCCCXIII
Let us find the total number of Is, Xs, and Cs, and group them starting from the largest landmark number.
Apparently, it looks like the largest landmark number is C, but note that 5 Cs (100s) make a D (500).
The efficiency of this system is due to the grouping of a given number by not just one group size, but a sequence of group sizes that we call landmark numbers.

$4$. Two $L$'s make a $C$ and one $L$ stays.
$5$. The sum is $CLXV$. Check with our numerals: $87 + 78 = 165$.
Answer: $CLXV$

$2$. Five $I$'s make a $V$, so now there are $3 V$'s: two of them make an $X$ and one $V$ stays.
$3$. That gives $6 X$'s: five make an $L$ and one $X$ stays, so now there are $3 L$'s.
$4$. Two $L$'s make a $C$ and one $L$ stays.
$5$. The sum is $CLXV$. Check with our numerals: $87 + 78 = 165$.
Answer: $CLXV$

content.text:
$1$. $V \times L$ is $5 \times 50 = 250$, which is $100 + 100 + 50$, written as $CCL$.
$2$. $L \times D$ is $50 \times 500 = 25000$, which is $25$ thousands, written as $M$ repeated $25$ times.
$3$. $V \times D$ is $5 \times 500 = 2500$, which is $1000 + 1000 + 500$, written as $MMD$.
$4$. $VII \times IX$ is $7 \times 9 = 63$, which is $50 + 10 + 1 + 1 + 1$, written as LXIII.
$5$. None of these products is a single landmark symbol, so there is no simple rule.
Answer: $V \times L$ is $CCL$, $L \times D$ is $25 M$'s, $V \times D$ is $MMD$ and $VII \times IX$ is LXIII

content.text: Identify the features of the Hindu number system that make it efficient when compared to the Roman number system.
content.question: Identify the features of the Hindu number system that make it efficient when compared to the Roman number system.
content.question_tex: Identify the features of the Hindu number system that make it efficient when compared to the Roman number system.
content.publication_text: Identify the features of the Hindu number system that make it efficient when compared to the Roman number system.

content.text:
$1$. Place value: in our numerals the position of a digit tells its landmark, so ten digits write every number; Roman symbols have fixed values and need new symbols for bigger numbers.
$2$. Zero: we have a digit $0$ for an empty place; the Roman system has no symbol for zero.
$3$. Calculation: adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing follow simple column rules in our system, while Roman numerals make them very hard.
Answer: Place value with ten digits, a symbol for zero, and easy calculation

content.text:
$1$. Look at your own system: does it need one mark for every object?
$2$. Add a group size: give a new symbol to a group, such as five marks.
$3$. Add landmark numbers: give new symbols to bigger groups too, such as five groups of five.
$4$. Write a few numbers in the refined system and check that they are shorter than before.

topics.summary: In the Egyptian system every landmark number is 10 times the one before, so the landmarks are 1, 10, 100, 1000 and so on, the powers of 10. A number is written with as many of each symbol as its grouping needs.

content.text:
3.3 The Idea of a Base
I. The Egyptian Number System: We are now going to see a written number system that the Egyptians developed around 3000 BCE.
Imagine making collections of pebbles. The first landmark number is 1. Group together 10 collections of the previous landmark number (1). Its size is the second landmark number which is 10. Group together 10 collections of the previous landmark number (10). Its size is the third landmark number which is 10 × 10 = 100, and so on.
Each landmark number is 10 times the previous one. Since 1 is the first landmark number, they are all powers of 10.
As in the case of Roman numbers, a given number is counted in groups of the landmark numbers, starting from the largest landmark number less than the given number.
For example 324 which equals 100 + 100 + 100 + 10 + 10 + 4 is written as three coils, two heels and four strokes.

content.text:
1. Predict first: if each new landmark is ten of the last, what comes after 1, 10 and 100?
2. Ten 1s make 10, ten 10s make 100, ten 100s make 1000: every landmark is a power of 10.
3. The Egyptians drew a stroke for 1, a heel for 10, a coil for 100, a lotus for 1000, and so on up to 10000000.
4. To write a number, take as many of the largest landmark as fit, then the next, and draw that many symbols.

content.text:
Worked example: Write 2153 in Egyptian numerals.
{{DIAGRAM:M2.S12.T12.C40.IMG2}}
1. The largest landmark that fits is 1000: two of them, 2153 − 2000 = 153.
2. One 100 fits: 153 − 100 = 53.
3. Five 10s fit: 53 − 50 = 3, which is three 1s.
4. So 2153 = 1000 + 1000 + 100 + 10 + 10 + 10 + 10 + 10 + 1 + 1 + 1.
5. It is written as 2 lotuses, 1 coil, 5 heels and 3 strokes.
Answer: 2 lotuses, 1 coil, 5 heels and 3 strokes

content.text:
Worked example: An Egyptian numeral shows 3 lotuses, 4 heels and 6 strokes. What number is it?
1. 3 lotuses: 1000 + 1000 + 1000 = 3000.
2. No coils, so no hundreds.
3. 4 heels: 10 + 10 + 10 + 10 = 40. 6 strokes: 6.
4. Total: 3000 + 40 + 6 = 3046.
Answer: 3046

<bookmark mark='land'/>The values one, five, twenty five and one hundred twenty five are called landmark numbers.

narration: <bookmark mark='km1'/>Kiko has one question to ask.
<bookmark mark='km2'/>What mistake do some students make here?
Some students think the answer is twenty eight squares and three triangles.
Twenty eight times five is one hundred forty, and three more is one hundred forty three.
So the total is right.
But five squares make one hexagon, and five hexagons make one circle.
So twenty eight squares become one circle and three squares, and we never keep five of one shape.

narration: <bookmark mark='km1'/>Kiko has one question to ask.
<bookmark mark='km2'/>What mistake do some students make here?
Some students think the landmarks are four, eight, twelve, sixteen, adding four each time.

topics.summary: A base-n system starts its landmarks at 1 and multiplies by the same n each time, so the landmarks are the powers of n. The Egyptian system is base 10; grouping by 5 gives a base-5 system with landmarks 1, 5, 25, 125.

content.text:
II. Variations on the Egyptian System and the Notion of Base
Instead of grouping together 10 collections of size equal to the previous landmark number (as in the case of the Egyptian system), can we get a number system by grouping together 5 collections of size equal to the previous landmark number? Can this 5 be replaced by any positive integer?
Group together 5 collections of size equal to the previous landmark number (1). Its size is the second landmark number which is 5.
Thus, we have a new number system where each landmark number is 5 times the previous one. Since 1 is the first landmark number, they are all powers of 5.
Express the number 143 in this new system. Let us start grouping, starting with the size 5³ = 125, as this is the largest landmark number smaller than 143. We get 143 = 125 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 1 + 1 + 1.

content.text:
Worked example: Write 89 in the base-5 system with triangle 1, square 5, hexagon 25 and circle 125.
{{DIAGRAM:M2.S15.T15.C47.IMG2}}
1. 125 is bigger than 89, so start with 25: three 25s fit, 89 − 75 = 14.
2. Two 5s fit in 14: 14 − 10 = 4, which is four 1s.
3. So 89 = 25 + 25 + 25 + 5 + 5 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1.
4. It is written as 3 hexagons, 2 squares and 4 triangles.
Answer: 3 hexagons, 2 squares and 4 triangles

content.text:
Number systems having landmark numbers in which the (a) first landmark number is 1, and (b) every next landmark number is obtained by multiplying the current landmark number by some fixed number n is said to be a base-n number system.
The Egyptian number system is a base-10 system, and the number system that we created is a base-5 system. A base-10 number system is also called a decimal number system.
The landmark numbers of a base-n number system are the powers of n starting from 1, n, n², n³, ...

content.text:
Worked example: Find the first five landmark numbers of a base-3 system and write 50 as a sum of them.
1. Start at 1 and multiply by 3: 1, 3, 9, 27, 81.
2. 81 is bigger than 50, so start with 27: one fits, 50 − 27 = 23.
3. Two 9s fit in 23: 23 − 18 = 5. One 3 fits: 5 − 3 = 2, which is two 1s.
4. So 50 = 27 + 9 + 9 + 3 + 1 + 1.
Answer: Landmarks 1, 3, 9, 27, 81; 50 = 27 + 9 + 9 + 3 + 1 + 1

{{DIAGRAM:M2.S16.T16.C51.IMG1}}

$2$. $137 = 125 + 5 + 5 + 1 + 1$: $1$ circle, $2$ squares and $2$ triangles.
$3$. $293 = 125 + 125 + 25 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 1 + 1 + 1$: $2$ circles, $1$ hexagon, $3$ squares and $3$ triangles.
$4$. $651 = 625 + 25 + 1$: $1$ wave, $1$ hexagon and $1$ triangle.

media.title: Is there a number the base five shapes cannot write?
media.context: A Story of Numbers. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: The row of base five shapes grows as far as we like, and ordinary counting numbers are all broken into it. Then the board asks what shape would stand for an empty collection, and finds there is none to draw.

video_script.why: The child uses the biggest-landmark-first method to see which numbers the base five shapes can write, and which cannot.

marks.ask: the question mark glows
marks.book: the title card From your book appears
marks.shapes: the row of shapes appears with a question mark after it

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about the base five shapes.
<bookmark mark='shapes'/>Each shape is worth five of the shape before it.
The row can grow as long as we like.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Is there a number that cannot be represented in our base five system above?
Why or why not?
beats.on_screen: small title card From your book; the row of base five shapes with values; a question mark after the row

marks.think: Kiko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.
beats.on_screen: the question stays on the board

marks.row: the row of landmarks keeps growing to the right
marks.count: a full collection and an empty collection appear side by side

narration: <bookmark mark='row'/>We write a number by grouping it into landmarks, the same way as the example in your book.
<bookmark mark='count'/>A number tells how many objects are in a collection.
A collection can also be empty.
beats.on_screen: the row of landmarks 1, 5, 25, 125, 625 continues to the right with dots; a collection of objects with an empty collection beside it

marks.given: the landmarks and the rule times five are written

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, shapes for one, five, twenty five and so on, each five times the one before.
beats.on_screen: Given: shapes for 1, 5, 25, 125, ... each 5 times the one before

marks.find: the question is written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to say whether some number cannot be written, and why.
beats.on_screen: To find: is there a number that cannot be written? Why?

marks.fit: the biggest landmark that fits is taken and subtracted
marks.down: the rest is smaller, so we move down to the next shape until triangles

narration: <bookmark mark='fit'/>Step one, take any counting number.
Take the biggest landmark that fits, and subtract it.
<bookmark mark='down'/>What is left is smaller than that landmark, so we move down a shape.
We stop at triangles, which are worth one each.
beats.on_screen: any counting number: biggest landmark that fits, subtract, move down; what is left is smaller than that landmark, so it ends at triangles

marks.big: a very big number appears past the end of the row
marks.new: a new shape worth five times the last one is added

narration: <bookmark mark='big'/>Step two, think of a number bigger than every landmark we have.
<bookmark mark='new'/>We only need a new shape, worth five times the last one.
We can always make one, so big numbers are never a problem.
beats.on_screen: a very big number needs a new landmark: 5 x (last landmark); new shape added to the row

marks.none: the empty box shows there is no shape to draw
marks.empty: the empty collection appears with the number 0

narration: <bookmark mark='empty'/>Step three, think of the number of objects in an empty collection.
That number is zero.
<bookmark mark='none'/>Every number in this system is written with at least one shape.
For zero there is nothing to draw.
beats.on_screen: 0 = number of objects in an empty collection; a number needs at least one shape; the shape for 0 is an empty box

marks.check: the numbers 1, 4 and 5 are matched to shapes, and 0 stays unmatched

narration: <bookmark mark='check'/>Step four, check with small numbers.
One is one triangle, four is four triangles, and five is one square.
Zero matches no shape at all.
beats.on_screen: check: 1 = 1 triangle; 4 = 4 triangles; 5 = 1 square; 0 = no shape

marks.rest: the numbers one to four are ticked as written

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Yes, zero cannot be written, because the system has no shape for it.
<bookmark mark='rest'/>Every other counting number can be written, however big it is.
beats.on_screen: Answer: Yes: 0 cannot be represented, because the system has no symbol for it

a number bigger than every symbol so far needs only a new landmark, 5 times the last
0 is the number of objects in an empty collection; every written number needs at least one shape; 0 has no shape
check: 1 is 1 triangle, 4 is 4 triangles, 5 is 1 square; nothing in the row stands for 0

media.title: What are the landmark numbers of a base seven system?
media.context: A Story of Numbers. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: The board builds the landmark numbers of a base seven system one step at a time, the way the base five shapes were built. Then the same steps are repeated with a base n, and the result is checked against base five.

video_script.why: The child uses the multiply-by-the-base method from the base three example to find the landmarks of base seven and of any base.

marks.ask: an empty row of five boxes labelled base 7 appears under it
marks.book: the title card From your book appears

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about the base seven system.
<bookmark mark='five'/>Here are the landmark numbers of base five.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Compute the landmark numbers of a base seven system.
In general, what are the landmark numbers of a base n system?
beats.on_screen: small title card From your book; the base five row 1, 5, 25, 125 with an empty row of five boxes under it labelled base 7

marks.think: Kiko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.
beats.on_screen: the question stays on the board with the empty row

marks.first: the first landmark is shown as a single dot
marks.group: a group of the base size is bundled into the next landmark
marks.seven: seven of a group are bundled into the next group

narration: <bookmark mark='first'/>In a base system, the first landmark is always one.
<bookmark mark='group'/>Each next landmark is a bundle of the base number of the landmark before.
<bookmark mark='seven'/>In base five, five bundles join to make the next one.
In base seven, seven bundles join.
beats.on_screen: ten of the first landmark group into the next in the Egyptian system; five of each group into the next in base five; seven of each group into the next in base seven

marks.given: base 7 and the first landmark 1 are written

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, a base seven system, where the first landmark is one.
beats.on_screen: Given: base 7; first landmark 1

marks.find: the two things to find are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the first five landmarks of base seven, and the landmarks of any base n.
beats.on_screen: To find: first five landmarks of base 7; landmarks of base n

marks.mult: the rule times 7 each time is written

narration: <bookmark mark='mult'/>Step one, start at one and multiply by seven each time.
<bookmark mark='seven'/>One times seven is seven.
<bookmark mark='forty'/>Seven times seven is forty nine.
<bookmark mark='third'/>Step two, keep multiplying by seven.
Forty nine times seven is three hundred forty three.
<bookmark mark='fourth'/>Three hundred forty three times seven is two thousand four hundred one.
That is the fifth landmark.

marks.gen: the base 7 is replaced by n
marks.pow: n times n is written as n squared and n squared times n as n cubed

narration: <bookmark mark='gen'/>Step three, do the same for any base n.
Start at one and multiply by n each time.
<bookmark mark='pow'/>We get one, then n, then n times n, which is n squared.
Next comes n cubed, and so on.
beats.on_screen: base n: start 1; 1 x n = n; n x n = n squared; n squared x n = n cubed

marks.five: the base five row is ticked against the rule
marks.four: 7 x 7 x 7 x 7 = 2401 is written and ticked

narration: <bookmark mark='five'/>Step four, check with base five.
One, five, twenty five and one hundred twenty five fit the rule for n equal to five.
<bookmark mark='four'/>Four sevens multiplied together also give two thousand four hundred one.
beats.on_screen: check with base 5: 1, 5, 25, 125 are the powers of 5; check with base 7: 7 x 7 x 7 x 7 = 2401

marks.ans: the five landmarks of base 7 are boxed
marks.gen: the powers of n are boxed

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Base seven has landmarks one, seven, forty nine, three hundred forty three, two thousand four hundred one.
<bookmark mark='gen'/>For any base, the landmarks are the powers of that base.
beats.on_screen: Answer: base 7: 1, 7, 49, 343, 2401, ...; base n: 1, n, n², n³, ..., the powers of n

video_script.anchor: the book's row of landmark numbers for base five, with an empty row waiting for base seven
video_script.design: One idea: landmarks multiply by the base. The empty row from the hook is filled in as the working goes along, and the base five row stays beside it for the check.
source: Figure it Out (base-n systems, question 3)
hold_back: 1, n, n², n³
maths_rules: base 7: the first landmark is 1; each next landmark is 7 times the one before
base n: 1, n, n x n = n squared, n squared x n = n cubed, and so on: the powers of n
check with base 5: 1, 5, 25, 125 are the powers of 5 (the book writes 5 to the power 0 = 1)
check with base 7: 7 x 7 x 7 x 7 = 2401, the fifth landmark
video_script.payoff_line: Base seven has landmarks one, seven, forty nine, three hundred forty three, two thousand four hundred one.

final_answer.value: Base 7: 1, 7, 49, 343, 2401, ...; base n: 1, n, n², n³, ..., the powers of n
final_answer.spoken: base seven has landmarks one, seven, forty nine, three hundred forty three, two thousand four hundred one, and for any base the landmarks are the powers of that base

video_script.substitution: Instead of three, the base is seven, and then the base is any number n.

media.teaching_notes: One idea: each landmark is the base times the one before, so the landmarks are the powers of the base. Watch for students who add the base each time instead of multiplying by it.

media.title: Can an Egyptian numeral use one symbol ten or more times?
media.context: A Story of Numbers. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: The board looks at what ten copies of one Egyptian symbol are worth, and why a numeral never keeps them. A number such as three hundred twenty four is used to check the idea.

video_script.why: The child uses the idea from the base five example, that five of a shape are always regrouped, for the Egyptian system with ten.

marks.ask: a question mark appears beside a long row of one repeated symbol
marks.row: the row of Egyptian symbols appears with their values
marks.book: the title card From your book appears

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about the Egyptian number system.
<bookmark mark='row'/>Each Egyptian symbol is worth ten of the symbol before it.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Can there be a number whose representation in Egyptian numerals

content.text: Is there a number that cannot be represented in our base$-5$ system above? Why or why not?
content.question: Is there a number that cannot be represented in our base-5 system above? Why or why not?

content.publication_text: Is there a number that cannot be represented in our base$-5$ system above? Why or why not?

content.text:
$1$. Every counting number can be grouped into powers of $5$, using each symbol at most $4$ times.
$2$. As numbers grow, we only need more landmark symbols, which can always be invented.
$3$. But $0$ is the number of objects in an empty collection, and there is no symbol to draw for it.
$4$. So $0$ cannot be represented.
Answer: Yes: $0$ cannot be represented, because the system has no symbol for it

content.text: Compute the landmark numbers of a base$-7$ system. In general, what are the landmark numbers of a base-$n$ system?
content.question: Compute the landmark numbers of a base-7 system. In general, what are the landmark numbers of a base-n system?
content.question_tex: Compute the landmark numbers of a base$-7$ system. In general, what are the landmark numbers of a base-$n$ system?
content.publication_text: Compute the landmark numbers of a base$-7$ system. In general, what are the landmark numbers of a base-$n$ system?

content.text:
$1$. Start at $1$ and multiply by $7$ each time: $1$, $7$, $7 \times 7 = 49$, $49 \times 7 = 343$, $343 \times 7 = 2401$.
$2$. In general, start at $1$ and multiply by $n$ each time.
$3$. So the landmarks of base $n$ are $1$, $n$, $n^2$, $n^3$, and so on, the powers of $n$.
Answer: Base $7$: $1$, $7$, $49$, $343$, $2401$, ...; base $n$: $1$, $n$, $n^2$, $n^3$, $\ldots$, the powers of $n$

In general, start at 1 and multiply by n each time.
So the landmarks of base n are 1, n, n², n³, and so on, the powers of n.

content.publication_text: Can there be a number whose representation in Egyptian numerals has one of the symbols occurring $10$ or more times? Why not?

content.text:
$1$. Every Egyptian landmark is $10$ times the one before.
$2$. If a symbol appeared $10$ times, those $10$ symbols would make exactly one symbol of the next landmark.
$3$. Grouping always takes as many of the larger landmark as possible, so the $10$ would be regrouped.
$4$. So no symbol is ever written $10$ or more times.
Answer: No: $10$ of any symbol make one of the next landmark, so they are always regrouped

content.text: Create your own number system of base $4$, and represent numbers from $1$ to $16$.
content.question: Create your own number system of base 4, and represent numbers from 1 to 16.
content.question_tex: Create your own number system of base $4$, and represent numbers from $1$ to $16$.
content.publication_text: Create your own number system of base $4$, and represent numbers from $1$ to $16$.

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M2.S17.T17.C59.IMG1}}
$1$. Landmarks of base $4$: $1$, $4$, $16$. Give them symbols, for example a dot for $1$, a stick for $4$ and a square for $16$.
$2$. $1$, $2$, $3$ are $1$, $2$, $3$ dots; $4$ is a stick; $5$, $6$, $7$ are a stick and $1$, $2$, $3$ dots.
$3$. $8$ is $2$ sticks; $9$, $10$, $11$ add $1$, $2$, $3$ dots; $12$ is $3$ sticks; $13$, $14$, $15$ add $1$, $2$, $3$ dots.
$4$. $16$ is one square, since four sticks make the next landmark.
Answer: Landmarks $1$, $4$, $16$; for example $7$ is a stick and $3$ dots, $12$ is $3$ sticks, $16$ is one square

narration: <bookmark mark='heels'/>Step one, count each kind of symbol together.
Heels come to eight plus seven, which is fifteen.
<bookmark mark='strokes'/>Strokes come to seven plus eight, which is also fifteen.
We add like symbols together, because each kind has its own value.

narration: <bookmark mark='swap'/>Step two, start with the smallest symbol.
Ten strokes make one heel, so fifteen strokes become one heel and five strokes.
<bookmark mark='sixteen'/>The heels are now fifteen plus one, which is sixteen.

narration: <bookmark mark='swap'/>Step three, move up to the heels.
Ten heels make one coil, so sixteen heels become one coil and six heels.
<bookmark mark='now'/>Every symbol is now used fewer than ten times, so we stop.
beats.on_screen: 16 heels = 1 coil and 6 heels

narration: <bookmark mark='values'/>Step four, check with ordinary numbers.
Eight heels and seven strokes is eighty seven, and seven heels and eight strokes is seventy eight.
<bookmark mark='check'/>Eighty seven plus seventy eight is one hundred sixty five.
So our coil, heels and strokes give the same total.

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The sum is one coil, six heels and five strokes, which is one hundred sixty five.

narration: <bookmark mark='powers'/>Step four, check base five.
A hexagon times a circle is five squared times five cubed.

<bookmark mark='check'/>Check by multiplying out.
Twenty five times a hundred is two thousand five hundred.
<bookmark mark='check2'/>Twenty five times twenty five is six hundred twenty five.
Together they make three thousand one hundred twenty five.

media.description: A numeral with a coil, two heels and a stroke is multiplied by ten, one symbol at a time, using the distributive property. The pattern is then used on a second numeral. Keeko's doubt is that only the biggest symbol moves up.

video_script.why: The child multiplies an Egyptian numeral by ten using the distributive property and finds the rule that every symbol moves up one landmark.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about multiplying Egyptian numerals.
<bookmark mark='sym'/>Here is a numeral with one coil, two heels and one stroke.

narration: <bookmark mark='next'/>A landmark times ten is the next landmark.
A stroke becomes a heel, a heel becomes a coil, and a coil becomes a lotus.
<bookmark mark='dist'/>The distributive property also works with more than two parts.
A sum times ten is each part times ten, added.

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to multiply it by ten, and then use the pattern for five hundred twenty two.

marks.times: each part is placed in brackets and multiplied by 10

narration: <bookmark mark='split'/>Step one, split the numeral into its landmarks.
A coil, two heels and a stroke are one hundred, ten, ten and one.
<bookmark mark='times'/>We multiply the whole sum by ten, so each part is multiplied too.

marks.dist: each part is multiplied by 10 separately
marks.vals: the four results 1000, 100, 100 and 10 are written

narration: <bookmark mark='dist'/>Step two, use the distributive property.
Multiply each part by ten on its own, because the distributive property says so.
<bookmark mark='vals'/>One hundred times ten is one thousand.
Ten times ten is one hundred, twice, and one times ten is ten.

marks.up: each symbol moves up one landmark: the coil to a lotus, the heels to coils, the stroke to a heel

narration: <bookmark mark='add'/>Step three, add the four parts.
We get one thousand two hundred ten, which is a lotus, two coils and a heel.
<bookmark mark='up'/>Look at the symbols.
The coil became a lotus, the two heels became coils, and the stroke became a heel.
So every symbol moved up one landmark.

narration: <bookmark mark='num'/>Step four, use the pattern for five hundred twenty two.
It is five coils, two heels and two strokes.
<bookmark mark='up'/>Move every symbol up one landmark, because each part is multiplied by ten.
We get five lotuses, two coils and two heels.
<bookmark mark='check'/>Check by value.
Five thousand plus two hundred plus twenty is five thousand two hundred twenty.

topics.summary: In a base the group size never changes, so adding regroups the same way at every step, and the product of two landmarks is a landmark. Multiplying by the base moves every symbol up one landmark.

content.text:
Advantages of a Base-n System
What is the advantage of having landmark numbers that are all the powers of a number? To understand this, let us perform some arithmetic operations using them.
Let us find the total number of strokes and heels and group them starting from the largest possible landmark number. It has a total of 15 heels and 15 strokes.
Since 10 heels gives the next landmark number, a coil, the sum can be regrouped.
I see a similarity in the method of adding numbers in the Egyptian and the Hindu system!
Contrast the addition done in a base-n number system with that done in the Roman system. In the Roman system, the grouping and rearranging has to be done carefully as it is not always by the same size that each landmark number has to be grouped to get the next one.

content.text:
How to multiply two numbers in Egyptian numerals? Let us first consider the product of two landmark numbers.
What is any landmark number multiplied by a heel (that is 10)?
Each landmark number is a power of 10 and so multiplying it with 10 increases the power by 1, which is the next landmark number.
Thus, the product of any two landmark numbers is another landmark number!
Does this property hold true in the base-5 system that we created? Does this hold for any number system with a base?

content.text:
1. Predict first: is 100 × 1000 one Egyptian symbol or many?
2. Multiplying a landmark by 10 gives the next landmark: 100 × 10 = 1000, a coil becomes a lotus.
3. Multiplying by 100 moves two landmarks up: 1000 × 100 = 100000, a lotus becomes a tadpole.
4. Landmarks are powers of the base, and a power times a power is a power, so this holds in every base, unlike in Roman numerals.

content.text:
Worked example: Find 100 × 10, 1000 × 100 and 100 × 1000 in Egyptian numerals, and check 25 × 125 in base 5.
{{DIAGRAM:M2.S18.T18.C61.IMG2}}
1. 100 × 10 = 1000: a coil times a heel is a lotus.
2. 1000 × 100 = 100000: a lotus times a coil is a tadpole.
3. 100 × 1000 = 100000: a coil times a lotus is also a tadpole.
4. In base 5, a hexagon times a circle: 25 × 125 = 3125, which is the arrow, another landmark.
5. In each case the product is a single landmark symbol.
Answer: A lotus, a tadpole, a tadpole, and in base 5 an arrow; each product is a landmark

content.text:
What can we conclude about the product of a number and a heel (10), in the Egyptian system?
Will the distributive property hold here? For the same reason that it holds for (a + b) × n, it also holds when one of the numbers has more than 2 terms. For example, (a + b + c) × n = an + bn + cn.
What would be a simple rule to multiply a number with a heel?
When the landmark numbers are powers of a number, then their product is another landmark number. This fact simplifies the process of multiplication.
Thus, a number system whose landmark numbers are powers of a number, i.e., a number system with a base, is efficient not only in number representation but also in its utility in carrying out arithmetic operations.

content.text:
1. Predict first: what happens to each symbol of 121 when the number is multiplied by 10?
2. Split the number into its symbols and multiply each one by 10: the distributive property.
3. Each symbol becomes the next landmark: a stroke becomes a heel, a heel a coil, a coil a lotus.
4. So the rule is: to multiply by 10, move every symbol up one landmark.

content.text:
Worked example: Multiply 121 (1 coil, 2 heels, 1 stroke) by 10, then use the rule to find 522 × 10.
{{DIAGRAM:M2.S18.T18.C62.IMG2}}
1. 121 = 100 + 10 + 10 + 1, so 121 × 10 = (100 + 10 + 10 + 1) × 10.
2. By the distributive property: 100 × 10 + 10 × 10 + 10 × 10 + 1 × 10 = 1000 + 100 + 100 + 10.
3. So 121 × 10 = 1210: 1 lotus, 2 coils and 1 heel; every symbol moved up one landmark.
4. 522 is 5 coils, 2 heels and 2 strokes; moving each up gives 5 lotuses, 2 coils and 2 heels, so 522 × 10 = 5220.
Answer: 121 × 10 is 1210 (1 lotus, 2 coils, 1 heel) and 522 × 10 is 5220

content.text:
Abacus that Makes Use of the Decimal System
In around the 11th century, even the people still using the Roman numerals started using a calculating device, the abacus, constructed using a decimal system.
Starting from the line that stood for 1, each successive line stood for a successive power of 10.
The presence of a counter above a line contributed a value of 5.
For example let us take the number 3426. It can be grouped as 3426 = 1000 + 1000 + 1000 + 100 + 100 + 100 + 100 + 10 + 10 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1.
Let us consider a simple addition problem: 2907 + 43. The two numbers were taken on either side of the vertical partition.
Hint: In this problem, the 7 ones and the 3 ones together make 10 ones which contributes a counter to the line representing 10s.

1. Predict first: when 7 ones and 3 ones come together on the board, what must happen?
2. Each line is a power of 10; a counter above a line is worth 5 of that line.
3. Bring the counters of the two numbers together line by line.
4. Ten counters on a line become one counter on the next line up, the same carrying as before.

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M2.S20.T20.C68.IMG1}}
$1$. (i): Strokes $8 + 7 = 15$: $1$ heel and $5$ strokes. Coils $6 + 5 = 11$: $1$ lotus and $1$ coil.
$2$. Lotuses $9 + 1 = 10$: $1$ finger. The sum is $1$ finger, $1$ coil, $1$ heel and $5$ strokes, which is $10115$. Check: $9608 + 507 = 10115$.
$3$. (ii): Strokes: $6$. Heels $8 + 4 = 12$: $1$ coil and $2$ heels.
$4$. The sum is $1$ lotus, $1$ coil, $2$ heels and $6$ strokes, which is $1126$. Check: $1080 + 46 = 1126$.
Answer: (i): $1$ finger, $1$ coil, $1$ heel, $5$ strokes, which is $10115$; (ii): $1$ lotus, $1$ coil, $2$ heels, $6$ strokes, which is $1126$

Lotuses 9 + 1 = 10: 1 finger. The sum is 1 finger, 1 coil, 1 heel and 5 strokes, which is 10115. Check: 9608 + 507 = 10115.
(ii) Strokes: 6. Heels 8 + 4 = 12: 1 coil and 2 heels.
The sum is 1 lotus, 1 coil, 2 heels and 6 strokes, which is 1126. Check: 1080 + 46 = 1126.

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M2.S20.T20.C70.IMG1}}
$1$. $2907$ has $2$ counters on the thousands line, $9$ on the hundreds line (one above it for $5$ and $4$ on it), none for tens and $7$ for ones; $43$ has $4$ tens and $3$ ones.
$2$. Bring the ones together: $7 + 3 = 10$ ones, which become $1$ counter on the tens line.
$3$. Tens: $4 + 1 = 5$, shown by one counter above the tens line.
$4$. Hundreds stay $9$ and thousands stay $2$, so the board shows $2950$.
Answer: $2950$

Tens: 4 + 1 = 5, shown by one counter above the tens line.
Hundreds stay 9 and thousands stay 2, so the board shows 2950.

media.description: Two numerals made of base five shapes are added by counting each kind of shape. The board looks for any shape that reaches five, and the sum is checked by value.

video_script.why: The child uses the count-and-swap method of the Egyptian addition in the base five system, where five of a shape make one of the next.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about adding in the base five system.
<bookmark mark='sym'/>A triangle is one, and a square is five.
<bookmark mark='sym2'/>A hexagon is twenty five, and a circle is one hundred twenty five.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Add the following numerals that are in the base five system that we created.
We must add one circle, two hexagons, one square and two triangles.
<bookmark mark='ask2'/>To it we add three circles, one hexagon, two squares and two triangles.
How many of each shape will the sum have?

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.
beats.on_screen: the question stays on the board with the empty box

marks.gather: the same kinds of shape are gathered together

narration: <bookmark mark='gather'/>We add as we did with Egyptian numerals.
We count each kind of shape together.
<bookmark mark='five'/>Here, five of a shape make one of the next shape.
Five is the count to watch for.

narration: <bookmark mark='squares'/>Step two, count the squares and the triangles.

content.text:
$1$. Each landmark times $5$ is the next landmark: $1 \times 5 = 5$, $5 \times 5 = 25$, $25 \times 5 = 125$.
$2$. By the distributive property, multiply every symbol of the number by $5$.
$3$. So every triangle becomes a square, every square a hexagon, every hexagon a circle, and so on.
$4$. Rule: replace each symbol by the symbol of the next landmark.
Answer: Replace every symbol by the symbol of the next landmark

topics.summary: A base needs a new symbol for every new landmark. The Mesopotamians grouped in powers of 60 and then dropped the landmark symbols: the position of each group tells whether it counts 1s, 60s or 3600s. That is place value.

content.text:
III. Shortcomings of the Egyptian System
If larger and larger numbers needed to be represented, then there was a need for inventing an unending sequence of symbols for higher and higher powers of 10.
3.4 Place Value Representation. I. The Mesopotamian Number System
In later times, it became a base-60 system, also called the sexagesimal system, with a very efficient number representation.
The influence of the Mesopotamian sexagesimal system, also known as the Babylonian number system, can be seen even now in our units of time measurements: 1 hour is 60 minutes and 1 minute is 60 seconds.
Note that we have actually used Indian numerals in creating these symbols.
Example: Let us represent the number 640 in this system. Grouping it into landmark numbers, we see that 640 = (10) × 60 + 40.
Example: Let us try another number, 7530. 7530 = (2) × 3600 + (5) × 60 + 30.

content.text:
1. Predict first: the Egyptians stopped at a symbol for 10000000; what happens to a bigger number?
2. Every new landmark in a base needs a new symbol, so the symbols never end.
3. The Mesopotamians grouped in powers of 60: 1, 60, 3600 and so on; we still use 60 in hours and minutes.
4. We borrow our numerals 1 to 59 for the count of each power of 60, like ten 60s and one 40 for 640.

content.text:
Worked example: Group 4000 into powers of 60 and say how it is written in base 60 with our own symbols.
{{DIAGRAM:M3.S22.T22.C75.IMG2}}
1. The landmarks are 1, 60 and 3600; 216000 is far too big.
2. One 3600 fits in 4000: 4000 − 3600 = 400.
3. Six 60s fit in 400: 6 × 60 = 360, and 400 − 360 = 40.
4. So 4000 = (1) × 3600 + (6) × 60 + 40.
5. It is written as 1 with the 3600 symbol, 6 with the 60 symbol, and 40.
Answer: 4000 = (1) × 3600 + (6) × 60 + 40

content.text:
Note that when a number is grouped into powers of 60 for its representation, no power of 60 can occur 60 or more times. If this happens, then 60 of them can be grouped to form the next power of 60.
(1) × 3600 + (70) × 60 + 2 = (1) × 3600 + (60 + 10) × 60 + 2 = (2) × 3600 + (10) × 60 + 2.
Therefore, any number can be represented using the numerals from 1 to 59, along with the numerals for landmark numbers.

1. Predict first: is 75 sixties allowed in a base-60 numeral?
2. 60 sixties make one 3600, so a count of 60 or more must be regrouped.
3. Take 60 out of the count and add 1 to the next landmark.
4. Every count then lies from 1 to 59.

content.text:
Worked example: Regroup (2) × 3600 + (75) × 60 + 10 so that no count is 60 or more.
1. 75 sixties is 60 sixties and 15 sixties.
2. 60 sixties make one 3600, so the 3600s go from 2 to 3.
3. So (2) × 3600 + (75) × 60 + 10 = (3) × 3600 + (15) × 60 + 10.
4. Both are 11710: 7200 + 4500 + 10 and 10800 + 900 + 10.
Answer: (3) × 3600 + (15) × 60 + 10, which is 11710

content.text:
Now, what if we make the representation even more compact by dropping the symbols for the different powers of 60 altogether?
This is exactly what the Mesopotamians did! In their numeral, the rightmost set of symbols showed the number of 1s, the set of symbols to its left showed the number of 60s, the next showed the number of 3600s and so on. Whenever there was no occurrence of a power of 60, a blank space was given in that position.
Such a number system (having a base) that makes use of the position of each symbol in determining the landmark number that it is associated with is called a positional number system or a place value system.
This idea of place value marks the highest point in the history of evolution of number systems.

1. Predict first: if the landmark symbols are dropped, how can a reader still tell 60s from 1s?
2. The place tells the landmark: rightmost 1s, next 60s, next 3600s.
3. So only the numerals 1 to 59 are needed, never a new symbol for a bigger landmark.
4. A system with a base where position gives the landmark is a place value system.

content.text:
Worked example: Write 3725 in the Mesopotamian place value system, using our numerals for each place.
1. One 3600 fits: 3725 − 3600 = 125.
2. Two 60s fit in 125: 125 − 120 = 5.
3. So 3725 = (1) × 3600 + (2) × 60 + 5.
4. Dropping the landmark symbols, it is written 1 | 2 | 5: 1 in the 3600s place, 2 in the 60s place, 5 in the 1s place.
Answer: 1 | 2 | 5, from 3725 = (1) × 3600 + (2) × 60 + 5

media.context: Class 8 NCERT Ganita Prakash ch 3 A Story of Numbers (Place Value and Zero). Leave a gap and the number collapses. Fix it with a zero. Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's board, the correct board, and the number line that explains the gap.
whatYouLearned: An empty column collapses and every digit to its left loses a place
A zero holds a place open and adds nothing to the total
Trailing zeros are needed for the same reason internal ones are

overview.goal: The student shows what goes wrong when a place is left empty instead of holding a zero, and states the rule for when a zero is needed.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A row of labelled place value columns with a digit tile tray beneath and a short number line under the readout. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class leaves the tens column empty and expects the board to still read the number they meant, and the board is asked to say what it actually reads.
overview.concept: In a positional system the place of a digit carries its value, so every place between the first digit and the last must be accounted for. Leaving a column empty does not record an absence, it removes the column, and the digits to its left slide down. A zero is the symbol that holds a place open without adding anything to the total.
overview.purpose: The student shows what goes wrong when a place is left empty instead of holding a zero, and states the rule for when a zero is needed.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Board across the upper main panel, readout directly beneath, number line under that. On a 390 px frame the column labels abbreviate but never disappear, and every tile keeps a 44 px hit target. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not show the readout while a prediction is still open, and never pad an empty column with a zero the student did not place. Padding would hide the whole phenomenon.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. The value of a digit is the digit times the power of ten for its column, and the column is fixed by counting places from the right. If a place is simply left out, everything to its left is counted from one place further right and so is worth ten times less. The zero contributes nothing to the sum but everything to the counting, which is why it is a placeholder rather than a quantity here. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.
